utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Monday, January the 19th. I'd like to greet the accused, the counsels, and particularly Mr. Khan, whom I'm pleased to see back. I would also like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, as well as all those present in the courtroom. I know that Mr. Registrar has a few IC numbers to provide me with, so I give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through witness Milan Cvikl. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit IC 00897. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC 00898. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC 00899. And the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC 00900. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar, for these IC numbers. First of all, I'd like to go to private session for a few moments -- to closed session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I hope you can hear me in your headphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask you to stand to pronounce the solemn declaration. Could you state your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] October the 30th, 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a job currently, and what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a historian, and I work at the Croatian Institute for History.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Already a witness before a court, whether national or international, on Yugoslavia or the former Yugoslavia, is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I witnessed before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a witness in the case Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were you a Prosecution or Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a witness for the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few brief pieces of information. Since you've already come to this Tribunal, you know how our proceedings take place. You'll have to answer questions which will be put to you by Mr. Stojic's counsels. I think Ms. Nozica will be doing the questioning, after which the other accused's counsels will cross-examine you. And after this, the Prosecution, who is on your right-hand side, may also cross-examine you. This is the procedure under our Rules. The four Judges before you at any time, and you will soon realise that, will be likely to ask questions to clarify aspects which may require so, so please be accurate in your answers. If you do not understand a question, do not hesitate to ask the one who posed it to rephrase it or to ask it again. For your information, today we shall bring the proceedings to an end at 1820, but for the coming days, the hearings will begin in the morning at 9.00. It is possible that in the light of the time used by Mr. Stojic's Defence and the other counsels' Defence, and on account of the time required by the Prosecution, we may not finish by Thursday, in which case you will have to stay at least until Monday, but let's be hopeful, and perhaps things will turn out better than expected. This is what I tell you, and I hope that if you have to stay, this will not cause you any serious inconvenience. Would there be a problem if you had to stay until Monday, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do have some family issues, but I do hope everything will be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also hope everything will be okay. And as I hope that everything will be okay, I give the floor, without further adieu, to Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Mr. Marijan. I would just like to provide you with several introductory technical remarks before I begin, but before that I would like to say that this is an expert witness, the first witness presented by the Defence of Mr. Stojic. As for my technical remarks, Your Honours, and the witness, you received four binders. There is a blue binder marked as binder X. In that binder, we have important organisational acts which we shall refer to on several occasions, and that's why they've been put into a separate binder. Moreover, there is a red binder containing this expert witness statement or report, rather, and there are also two binders containing different documents. We've provided you also with the expert witness's report that he gave in the previous case, so that the Chambers may, if they wish, check whether both of these reports touch upon the same issues and whether he's testifying in the same manner. With Your Honours' indulgence, and obviously with the indulgence of my learned friends from the Prosecution, before we start with the topic of this report, I would like to very quickly go through the curriculum vitae and the expertise of this witness, and his scientific work. I believe that this might be very important so that we'll learn what is the extent of knowledge of the witness before he started -- what it was before he started working on his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marijan, I will kindly ask you, as I'm often asked in this courtroom, if I start speaking too quickly when asking questions, and you should also be mindful of this when you are answering, we have to speak rather slowly in order for the Judges to be able to understand us. That's a very important reason. But there's also the second reason, and this is the gentleman taking minutes, the transcript, should be able to record everything, and the interpreters should also be able to do their job. Just a few questions regarding your work experience. In your CV, we can see that you participated in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period between 1992 and 1995 as a member of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I participated as a volunteer on three occasions in HVO units in the period between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is also stated here that you were a member of the Petar Kresimir 4th Brigade in Livno. Could you tell me where you were based and what were your tasks? Where was this brigade based, and who HVO was in conflict with at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I was a member of this brigade in 1992. This brigade was continuously based an in the territory of the Municipality of Livno. I was a member of the Students' Company of this brigade, and I was an infantry soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been warned that in line 1 of the transcript, a year is missing. That was my question. So in my question, I referred to the year 1992, and I would like to thank my colleague for this warning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my answer, I did refer to the year 1992, and I can only add that at that time we were at war with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your CV, we can also see that you were a member of the 1st Brigade, Petar Kresimir the 4th in Livno between July 1992 [as interpreted] and April 1994. Could you please tell me where you were stationed at the time and what were your tasks?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: If you allow me, in line 12 it says "July 1992." Well, that was actually July 1993. I was a member of the same brigade. I was the commander of the Students' Company. That was the time of the war with Muslims. Most of the time I spent in this brigade, I was at positions facing the Bosnian Serbs, and I believe that on three occasions I was in another place for periods of ten days each time. This was in the area of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The fourth time you came to Livno, the fourth time you came, where were you then?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This was the third time. Then I was a member of a professional unit of the 1st Guards Brigade of the HVO. I was a member of this brigade between September 1994 and the end of July or August 1995. At that time, I was in charge of the political activity in the department of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you said you were a volunteer and you came to Livno. Could you please explain to this Court, what does this mean? So at the time of your first coming in April 1992, where was your permanent residence, what is your origin, when and why you came to Livno on the three occasions mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: At the time, I was a student. I studied in Zagreb. I lived then and I still live in a small town in the vicinity of Zagreb called Velika Gorica. Just before I began my studies, my father built a house there, and this is where I've lived. I went to Livno on three occasions, frankly speaking, because of my parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What does that mean, because of your parents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: It was war. The war was on, and my feeling was that had I not gone down there when my family was endangered, I could have never faced coming there again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you went because you could not have faced going down there again in the future had you not gone on that occasion. Did I understand this well?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So we are talking about April 1992. Who was endangering your family at the time in Livno?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: My family was in danger because of the army at the time. It was still called Yugoslav People's Army. Later, it was renamed into the Army of the Republika Srpska. My village was at the very front-line facing this army, and the attack started just a few days after I came there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will try to go very quickly through your scientific expertise and your work experience, which is very significant, also significant for your report. You said that you completed your studies of history and archaeology at the Faculty of Philosophy in 1994; that you gained Master's of Arts degree at the same faculty in January 2005, with a thesis: Ustasha military units, 1941 to 1945; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You got your Doctoral degree on May 11th, 2006, with the thesis entitled: "Yugoslav People's Army and the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, 1987 to 1992"; is this also correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Between December 1992 and September 2001, you worked at the Central Military Archives and the Military Museum of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, although they had me officially working at the Military Museum for a year, although I actually worked at the Central Military Archives at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you worked at the scientific project "Creation of the Republic of Croatia and Croatian War of Independence, 1991 to 1995 to 1998," in the period between 2001 and 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Your CV says that since 2007, you've been working as a researcher and head of the scientific project: "The Republic of Croatia and the Homeland War, 1991 to 1995"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Furthermore, it says that in the summer of 2000, you participated in drafting of the complaint of the Republic of Croatia against the Federal State of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Furthermore, it says that following a request of the Government of the Republic of Croatia's Office for Cooperation with the ICTY, you were in The Hague, you informed the Prosecution teams with the significance of the war activities against the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I don't remember the name of the person for -- working for the investigative teams. I was offered at the time to work for them as an expert, but at the time I believed that my knowledge was not satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I hope that today you believe your knowledge is satisfactory to testify as a witness.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, but I need to mention that I've been interested in the Yugoslav People's Army for a long time. I had information coming from the media, the documents, and as we compiled the complaint against Yugoslavia, I had an opportunity to come across a huge amount of documents that were created by that army and which were before kept by the security services. I need to say that as -- that I found reading these documents very hard, and the picture that I used to have about the Yugoslav People's Army changed pretty drastically. So after 2005, I gained sufficient expertise to witness about this subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Furthermore, it says that ever since 2002, you've been an editor of the "Polemos" publication?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, this is the only publication in Croatia that deals with this subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do many times already before, and let me ask you, Madam Nozica, to be really slowing down and making a pause between your question, and we ask the witness, Mr. Davor Marijan, to wait a bit when you receive the question and then answer it slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have also noticed that you are starting with your answers too soon. Please do wait for the interpretation of the question before you start with your answer. Furthermore, it is stated here that after spring 2003, you've been an adviser on the archive in the Council for Military Property of the MOD of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is also stated here that you published seven books. Six of them are monographies. Could you, Mr. Marijan, please mention the titles of these books so if anybody is interested -- if anybody is interested in further details, they might ask that later on.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Maybe it might be better if I said that these books regard the period of the Second World War and of the war between 1991 and 1995. I focused in particular on one of the battles, the Battle for Vukovar. I also focused on two brigades, on one army, one particular military operation, the Storm, in 1995, one battle from the Second World War. And in one of the last books, there are some articles I wrote regarding the last war, the war between 1991 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You did not list the titles, but did you write the book titled: "The Collapse of Tito's Army and the Breakdown of Yugoslavia from 1992 through 1995"? And as far as I see, the book was published by the Croatian History Institute in Zagreb in 2008; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is, in fact, my amended Doctoral thesis. It was published by two publishers. One of them was my institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, can you say a few words about your scholarly work? I have a list of 24 papers of yours, but as we must proceed rather slowly, I'm afraid that we will -- this will take much time, although this is very important. So could you please summarise what is most important with regard to the subject matter of this expertise? What were your papers about?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the subject matter of my papers is the same as that of my books. Some are about the Second World War, most of them about this war. They deal with military issues, organisational issues, combat. In brief, they all deal with war and the military. And let me just add that they are all original scholarly works or papers that I worked at myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let us now go into the topic that has directly to do with your expertise and your work. Let me first ask you about the documentation that you took into consideration. How did you come by the documentation, which was the foundation for your work? Who gave it to you and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question. I have listened carefully to the answers that you've given to Madam Nozica's questions regarding your curriculum vitae, and what I can say at this point is that you were a member of a fighting brigade in Livno, and therefore you have experience, first-hand experience of the war. I also notice that you've studied history, which enabled you to write a number of articles, and also you were fortunate to work in the Military Archives, which enabled you to have access to documentation. Myself and the other Judges have read through your report that will be discussed during the questioning phases, but the question that comes to mind, which I would like to put forward at this point so that you understand exactly what the Chamber expects from you, is as follows: At the time, that is, 1992-1993, there was a Department of Defence with a minister of defence, and on-site there were a number of military leaders like Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Coric and others, and unfortunately there were a number -- there were persons who were the victims of military actions. This Court, this Chamber, must examine the responsibility of the minister of defence at that time in order to determine how the minister of defence or whether the minister of defence had authority over the military personnel, whether he had any power to sanction under Article 7.3 of the present Tribunal, what his relationship was with Mr. Boban and Mr. Prlic, and how the command structure functioned. Those are the issues. Those are the main questions that we must deal with. Perhaps in your responses, you can contribute to clarifying these matters, in particular the points that I have just mentioned, and I wanted to let you know what we're expecting in advance because perhaps you can answer the questions I have just put forward in your responses. Would you be able to confirm that you, as an expert, are able to answer these various questions that I have just put forward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to question my own expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, fine, thank you. We are all expecting what's coming up. Go ahead, Madam Nozica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence counsel, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you for your instructions and remarks, and it is the very same issues that you mentioned that we will also devote time to. Let me just technically pass through what I consider rather important; namely, to see which documents this expert witness had in front of him and that were the foundation for the conclusions of his work.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, Witness, please do allow a little time to elapse after I finish my question and before you answer.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tend to speak fast, but I'll try to keep that in mind. My work is based on the documents that are received from the Defence, the documents that are received from the Defence and are on the list from the Prosecution. And let me say that research into the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina is part of my job description, as it were, so that even earlier in my previous testimony a few years ago, I did have access to documents in the HVO archives which are in the Croatian National Archive, and in most of the documents I was shown had been known to me from previous times. And of course all my work is based strictly on documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, did you have a chance to read the works of other experts in military matters or experts in other subject matter that I will ask you about and who have testified before this Court? More specifically, are you familiar with the work or the paper and all the documents mentioned by Expert Witness Pringle in this case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Pringle's expert opinion. I received it from you. And I also read some expert opinions by witnesses who testified here. These are expert opinions from witnesses in Belgrade, from the Helsinki Human Rights Committee of Serbia, and some of those opinions I took great interest in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You did not reply to my question, whether you read every single document mentioned by Expert Witness Pringle before this Court.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I apologise for not replying precisely. Yes, I did, I did read all the documents from the list that was attached.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who did you contact while working on your expert opinion, talking about the Defence team of Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I contacted you and a member of your team, an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did anybody influence you regarding the conclusions of your expert opinion? Did anybody suggest to you that you should draw up conclusions that are contrary to your conviction?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the conclusions are exclusively mine, and nobody tried to influence me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Can you now tell the Court, and now we are going on -- or now we are about to deal with your expert opinion. I'll proceed in a chronological manner, and we'll try to deal with things in the same way that you laid them out in your opinion. We have singled out a smaller number of documents than can be found in your footnotes, and now I would like to ask you whether the documents mentioned in your footnotes, and that we will not show here, whether those documents are those documents that -- upon which your expert opinion is entirely based.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, those are the documents upon which my opinion is based.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, what was the topic of your expert opinion, specifically?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The topic of my opinion was the position of the Department of Defence in the framework of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, as well as the position of the head of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is that limited to a certain period?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: It is limited by the role of the head of the department, so there was a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me now ask you to take a binder. I believe it's the red binder that contains your expert opinion. Please open it. Can you now say precisely which period we are talking about? Do mention dates.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: We're talking about the period from the 3rd of July, 1992, until about the 15th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have a semantic problem here. You have just mentioned the head of the department. When you refer to the head of the department, what is the difference between the head of the Department of Defence and the minister of defence? Is there a difference, in your mind? And if so, what is the difference, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a difference between these two. "Head of department" means that the body in question is a provisional body, which is not at the level of a ministry. So it's a lower-level body and a body whose name suggests that it is provisional. That can be also concluded from some basic acts passed by the Herceg-Bosna when it was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the individual who carries out the same functions as the head of the Department of Defence, but it's not a temporary structure, is it then the minister of defence, is that person the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think in that case the individual would be called the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I could just ask one question. I take it to be the result of your answers that the practical functions were the same of a chief of department or ministries; it was just the general framework, the structure, that changed, but he did the same thing, same office, same binders, same people he worked with, same competencies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Department of Defence is a similar function, but as I said, it is provisional or temporary. I was able to hear some interpretations that the department is considered like an outpost of a ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask you one more question, Witness. When a Judge asks a question, we have a very open approach. There is no trap. You must keep that in mind. These are questions that which aimed at obtaining information. So we have a very open, neutral approach, and the only purpose is to find the truth and understand exactly what occurs, and there is no trap and we're not taking sides. So when I or one of the other Judges ask you a question, please understand that we are simply trying to find the truth. That is our approach; whereas obviously the Defence has its opinion, and the Prosecution has its opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. My hesitation may have been interpreted as an attempt to contrive something, but although I try to be slow, I may still be faster than the official court reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't worry. I am able to follow in realtime. It's my colleague who prefers that there be breaks in between the questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, I can see that this technical issue of the transcript is becoming very important to you. It may distract you, so let me just say relax, just make a break, allow some time to elapse between question and answer. And you did reply to many of the questions just asked by the Judges in your expert opinion, but nonetheless we will make a leap forward, because there's something you deal with later. Did you, sir, have a chance to see the documents, any documents, and whether according to those documents that you saw, Mr. Stojic was minister and the Ministry of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna when it was established? So did you see any mention in documents that he was appointed to that function? I'm asking this because Judge Trechsel asked you whether those were the -- whether the secretary of defence did the same business as a minister. And dealing with this topic, did you -- was that an issue that you dealt with at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not research into the period after Mr. Stojic left his position. I have never seen a document appointing him minister of defence, but I did see some documents signed by him with the title of minister, but I never saw an appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That is a correct answer. Mr. Marijan, you are saying that you have not seen the appointment of Mr. Stojic as a cabinet member of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us go back to your expert opinion. In the introductory remarks, you state something very significant; namely, that you have not seen log-books -- the log-books of Mr. Stojic. Is this important information that should have been mentioned in such an expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that this is important information. I do not doubt that the approach of the Tribunal, the legal approach, and the approach of a historian differ. I, as a researcher, know that especially young researchers, when they first go to archives, their first encounter with the documents there starts with the log-book or ledger, so that the servers that run the archives, that is, the staff working there, first offer you the log-book. It's a book containing all the entries, everything that was done in that context. I must say that I never look for that in the archives in which I work, because it is my habit of going through all the documents because my experience shows that if you look at the documents without previous bias, you will get additional impulses for further work, and that is fruitful. And -- but when you take a log-book, then you will see a reliable list of documents which the person who compiled that, the entirety of the documentation received. In other words, it's a summary of all the work done on those documents, on that documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But what you have just said is something of a definition of a log-book, or should we add some more information to this definition?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The log-book, Your Honours, is something like an inventory of the creator of a collection, which includes all the mail received, all documents received. Talking about military cases, there are usually several log-books. It is customary that these log-books are kept separate because the documentation contained has different levels of secrecy. It starts with the first day of a year and ends with the last day of that same year. Those would be official log-books.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we then immediately establish -- please take a look at the first binder. It should be down there someplace. Document 2D 1399. Your Honours, this is the first binder on your desk, 2D 1399. This is a letter from the assistant minister of justice of Croatia. Does it follow from this letter that the Defence of Mr. Stojic requested the log-book and that it wasn't found? Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this letter, and that is indeed what follows from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Does it follow from it that the log-book was searched for in several archives or, rather, only those archives where it could possibly be?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Well, they searched for it in the Military Archive of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, although it couldn't have possibly been there. The only archive it could have been in is the Croatian National Archive, because that's where the archives of the HVO are -- the HVO are kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. This now reads: "The Department of Defence in the System of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." This is the first chapter of your expert opinion. So the Presidency of the HZ-HB as a legislative body in 1992 passed two decisions that are very important for your expert opinion and important for determining the position of the Department of Defence and its head in that system. Could you please tell the Court which two decrees these are?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are two decrees with the same title; namely, "The Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." One was passed on the 3rd of July, 1992, and the second one on the 17th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will ask you very briefly about the second one. It was, in fact, an amendment to the first one?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is an amendment and a supplement to the first one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you answer me, Mr. Marijan, what were the responsibilities, duties and obligations of the head of Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the duties and responsibilities of the head of the Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna are grouped into three categories.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Marijan. We're talking about the armed forces here.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Right, the armed forces. So the first was leading and commanding the armed forces. The second group of his responsibilities and duties related to the staffing policy and the manning of the armed forces. And the third group related to the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we should clarify whether we're talking about the minister of defence or if we're talking about somebody else here, because I think the record doesn't make it very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. I thought I was rather clear. I can't follow the transcript at the same time, but we are talking about the responsibilities and duties of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. If you want the name to be quite clear, it was Mr. Boban. Those are the duties and responsibilities of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes. I understood you very well. I understood you as asking about the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Don't worry about the transcript. I will ask for a correction. Do not be distracted. So let's emphasise once again, we are talking about the powers of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, according to the provisions of the decree of the 3rd of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, could you tell us which number we can find this decree under, because I'd like to have a look at the actual text.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I will show all these decrees later. It is P2000289 [as interpreted]. It's in the X binder, P000289. Those are all the founding documents that are relevant for this part of the questioning. To facilitate the work of the Bench, I'll give you the number of the second decree. It's P000588. It was passed in the same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened with the second decree? Did it extend the powers of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The supplemented -- the amended decree increased the powers of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, as I stated in paragraph 2 of my report. And I can read it, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just what you believed to be important. Don't go into detail, because we have your report. Anyone who wants to know more will easily come back to it. What we are interested in are the powers of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: These provisions are very interesting to me, very curious, the possibility to mobilise even minors and the possibility to form a commission to supervise the work of the Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me precisely now what are the obligations and powers of the supreme commander of the armed forces, according to these provisions, that is, the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? You told us about his power to lead and command the armed forces. First of all, we'll specify the article in these two decrees that governs this. Tell us about the first decree first, and what were the key powers granted him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: In both decrees, the first decree and the amended decree, the key responsibilities are in Article 29. There is an enumeration of seven responsibilities and powers of the president, Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what was in items 2, 3 and 7?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Boban had the authority to adopt a plan of use and employment of armed forces. The plan of employment is, in some countries, called "the war plan." In item 3, he provided guide-lines for taking measures of readiness and mobilisation of the armed forces, and under 4 he was the main architect of the staffing policy in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Does item 7 confirm this, which is more specific?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes. It is part of that, in a way, appointing and relieving of duty of military commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at Article 29, I'd be interested in number 2 most particularly, because there are seven tasks to be performed by the supreme commander, and I'm interested in task number 2. I have the impression, reading Article 29(2), that it is Mr. Boban himself who approves and orders armed force operations, armed forces operations. Do you share this interpretation of all the documents we have looked into? Because I'm talking about this particular instrument, but it is something which is very important for us to find out. Imagine in a municipality X, there is a military operation carried out by a combatting unit. Why for, say, in Livno, for the purposes of this, for the purposes of this military operation, is it Mr. Boban at the very top who needs to approve the operation? Let me clarify the question. If there is a military operation, not a defensive military operation but an offensive military operation, in such a case is it the supreme commander who's giving the approvals, giving the green light, and who approves the plan developed, for example, by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Before answering the question asked by the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, I would like also to add as a follow-up question, the following: That we have here, of course, originally the question relates to what Madam Nozica asked, yes, Article 29, and which is about the command and control of the armed forces; but as I have looked at Article 10, I believe that the two articles should be read in a way together, because Article 10 speaks about the executive bodies of the HZ-HB and Defence Department, and then if we have a look at the different departments' activities, it says: "The department shall engage in activities pertaining to ..." It is actual on page 14, page 14, Article 10. Then we will see here that monitoring and coordination of activities to implement and establish defence policy and the proposing of measures for its development and implementation. And then, actually, sub-para 3 says: "The formulation of a plan for the deployment of the armed forces," and then 4: "The systems of command and control of the armed forces ...," et cetera, et cetera. So my question is a follow-up to President Antonetti's question. What, in your view, is the interconnection and relationship of Articles 10 and 29, and what are the roles both of, in this case, the supreme commander of the armed forces, which was then Mr. Boban, and, of course, the department -- Defence Department headed by the head of the department? So it is my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness. Your Honours -- Your Honour Mr. Prandler, if you allow me, we will deal very soon with Article 10, the witness and I. It's a very important article governing the responsibilities and obligations of the head of Department of Defence, and I believe it will be much easier for the expert to understand your question if we go through the previous three pages in this document. But if I may, Presiding Judge Antonetti asked a question about Article 29, a very precise and very interesting question, but I believe the expert can answer but I would to ask the witness to take binder X and have Article 29 before him so that he can give a precise answer to Judge Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you may have been puzzled by my colleague's question, or perhaps my question was not as clear as it should have been. Let me repeat this. This question of my colleague may have caused some confusion for you because my question was not clear. Of course, I've already seen Article 10, but my question is not on Article 10. My question relates to Mr. Boban, and I wanted to know if it is Mr. Boban, himself, who had to give his approval to an offensive military operation. And perhaps you could take an example -- or the example I took was Livno, because you may have experienced that yourself. So when your unit was in an offensive operation, your commander says, Well, tomorrow morning we'll move to that-and-that location five kilometres away, with, of course, the risk of combatting activities, and I wanted to know if such decisions were taken by Mr. Boban himself, under the paragraph, "Command and Control," if Mr. Boban himself was actually giving the green light to such operations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood you well both the first and second time. Your question was quite specific. Now, let me say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually, my questions are crystal clear and everyone understands them, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this -- on this point, I would like to say what the plan of employment of armed forces is. The plan of employment, generally speaking in every army, is a contingency document. One should not consider that if you have a plan for wartime, and I'm speaking as someone coming from Croatia, if, for instance, Croatia has a war plan for a war with Serbia or with Slovenia, both neighbouring countries, does not -- that plan does not mean that an aggression is planned. It's just a preventative measure. However, the plan of defence is more specific. A plan can be defensive or offensive. Speaking of defensive plans, what can happen is that you are attacked suddenly by surprise. In that case, a military commander cannot afford to ask for approval from his superior. He must immediately respond to the attack. However, if we are talking about an offensive plan in a system that claims to be well structured, the rules are very clear. In this specific case, it would mean that a war plan had been prepared in Livno or covering Livno as part of a larger operation. That plan would have been made in the Main Staff, but it would have been approved by President Boban. That would be the ideal scenario. That's the only way we can read this paragraph, this article. But I must confess I have not seen the plan of employment of armed forces, as it is defined here, nor can I remember that Mr. Boban had approved any offensive actions in any documents, which is easily understandable, because the main characteristic of the HVO was that it was a defensive force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what you're saying is very important, because this trial has been taking place for about two years and -- this is, of course, my personal point of view. I don't know if my colleagues share my view. But you have, in my view, made a distinction of tremendous importance, and that's why I asked my question. It was an open question for you to answer some question marks, the plan was offensive, already offensive. And that's really my question, you've added something which we've heard here for the first time, as far as I know; that is, that according to you, the HVO never carried out offensive actions, but had always had a defensive policy, and you've also added that you had never seen any document on offensive action with Mr. Boban's name. This is what you answered earlier on, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do need to clarify, Your Honour. The system that is the basis of my military education, the system I dealt with, uses the terms "defensive" and "offensive" in a strategic sense. That means moving the entire army or the bulk of the army. That kind of plan is something I have not seen in the HVO. I have seen offensive activity by the HVO, but on a tactical level. That means minor forces, but I have not seen it on a strategic level. That means I'm not saying the HVO never attacked, but all that was on a lower tactical level. And let me be quite clear, I mean the period covered by my report. Later, in the years 1994 and 1995, I've also seen major --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take a specific military example. Say there's the front-line, the enemy cross it, and the friendly forces are on one side. The friendly forces, the HVO, for example, have a general defensive policy, a general policy which is defensive. Imagine they realise that across the line, a mortar has been moved by the enemy to a higher location on a hill, and therefore there is an obvious military risk. So the HVO decides to attack the hill to take that mortar which may pose a threat at a later stage, so the hill is under attack. Now, this HVO offensive, would it be considered as the implementation of a defensive policy, and the offensive activity can be considered as a preventative operation, so this offensive operation in such a case, should it be interpreted as part of the overall defensive strategy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the example you set out, in military terminology we would use the term "active defence." It could be -- it may be part of a defensive strategy, but I must admit I dealt for a long time -- I've been dealing a long time with an army with a well-developed strategy. However, the problem with the HVO is that it lacks what we call doctrinary documents, and any conclusions on its strategy can only be made by analysing its activity. There is no other basis for making conclusions about their strategy. That's why I'm saying that the main thrust of the HVO was defence. Even after 1993, HVO is what we called blocking defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can follow, but you'll agree with me that this is quite complicated, because between active defence, blocking defence, and all those concepts, one may get lost. But I do understand, but I wonder if everybody's still with you. Should you not define or clarify some concepts? Earlier on, you said that the HVO did not have any doctrine document. I'm astonished at this, because a lot of HV [as interpreted] officers were former high-ranking officers of the JNA, so the military doctrine, they knew all about it. So why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that for the simple reason because I haven't seen any. I frankly doubt that a document of that nature could exist without me seeing it. The Yugoslav People's Army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... because usually I don't look at the transcript in English, because I cannot look at you and look at everybody and at the same time look at the screen. But it was by mere chance, and I happened to see the English text. And since this is a very complex and difficult field, at line number 8, I said that the HV officers were former JNA officers, not Croatian Army officers, because in English it said "the HV." I said "the HVO," and one may think that it was the Croatian Army on the spot, and I didn't go that far and draw that conclusion. What I said is that HVO officers, at least some of them, were former JNA officers. So line 8, it's not "HV officers" but "HVO officers." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the former Yugoslav Army, in its 40 or so years of peacetime, had five doctrine-establishing documents of this nature that determined and chart the doctrine. I have to emphasise that a picture is being painted, and I cannot agree with that picture, that a large number of trained JNA officers - and when I say "trained officer," I mean a person who graduated from the Military Academy - were numerous in the HVO. Such people were very few, in fact, in the HVO. And in the period I'm dealing with, you cannot say that these people occupied high positions. The highest reach of these officers was commanding a battalion or an artillery battalion, so that in terms of staffing, out of all the armies in Western Herzegovina and Croatia, not to name them all, the HVO had the greatest number of trained officers, which we can see from the documents. And I did do comparative analysis. I hope none of the accused will take this against me. But the HVO had the poorest -- the weakest combat documents, which is an indicator of the level of educational attainment, and training of the entire officers' cadre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a question or shall we have the break? My colleague has a follow-up question, and then we shall have a break, because otherwise the cafeteria is going to be closing, and it will be too late. I say this turning to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a question which might in a way be a summing up of this last discussion. According to Article 29, paragraph 2, Mate Boban has the power to draw up a plan for the operation of the armed forces. In fact, he never drew up such a plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can say that I have not seen it, I cannot guarantee 100 per cent, but when it comes to such plans, when a general plan is drafted, obviously certain things are delegated. In the former system, this was done by a decree, and this was delegated all the way to the level of a brigade. So there should have been a trace from that period somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to counsel, I'd like to read out a decision. I'm going to be reading it slowly. I know the interpreters do not have a copy of the text, and it's a bit long. Oral decision regarding the request submitted by the Petkovic Defence. In order to appeal or certify appeal of the oral decision made by the Chamber, the Chamber has received a submission dated 14th January 2009 by the Petkovic Defence in which they request that the Chamber re-examine or to certify appeal of the oral decision made January 12th, 2009, by the Chamber. In this oral decision dated January 12th, 2009, the Chamber has decided the following: Proprio motu, not to authorise the Petkovic Defence to use two and a half additional hours in order to question the expert witness, Davor Marijan, over and beyond the additional time which has already been granted by the Chamber to the Petkovic Defence; that is, one hour and thirty minutes. At the January 14th, 2009 hearing, the Chamber ordered the parties to present their submissions in response as of January 16th, at the latest. On January 16th, 2009, the Praljak Defence presented a submission in which they state they have joined the initial request presented by the Petkovic Defence. In addition, on the same day the Stojic Defence and the Prosecution have presented a filing in response, in which they oppose the Petkovic Defence's request. Having examined these submissions presented by the parties, and having deliberated and discussed it, the Chamber decides to reject the request for the following reasons: First of all, as regards the request to reconsider, in keeping with directive number 5 of the decision made April 24th, 2008, if a Defence team wants additional time for the cross-examination of the witness, it must justify such request in writing, and it is up to the Chamber to determine the length of time for cross-examination on the basis of this request and on the basis of the lists that have been submitted, in keeping with Article 65 ter of the Rules and Regulations. Although the Chamber agrees with the Petkovic Defence that indeed the Chamber has authorised since the beginning of the Defence case, the Defence teams have used their own time to present their case to cross-examine other witnesses, we must nonetheless note that the request for time on the part of the Defence teams is unreasonable. In particular as, indicated in the contested decision, the request for additional time made by the Petkovic Defence is excessive, inasmuch as it modifies substantially the overall schedule of the hearing of the Stojic Defence and would extend the cross-examination of the expert witness in a way that is contrary to the requirements of a fair and equitable trial. In not authorising the Petkovic Defence to use additional time, over and beyond the additional time which has already been granted by the Chamber, to cross-examine the witness Davor Marijan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Davor Marijan, the interpreter makes the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is not intervening, contrary to what the Petkovic Defence states, in the determination of the Petkovic Defence strategy, but is simply using its power and its duties to control the organisation of the examination of a witness in order to provide that the accused benefit from a speedy and equitable trial. The circumstances relating to additional time requested by the Petkovic Defence would correspond to time which would be taken away from the time used to present his own case, and that does not go against the pre-mentioned conclusion. The Chamber, therefore, does not see any reason to reconsider the oral decision handed down January 12th, 2009. Secondly, as regards the request to certify appeal, the Chamber recalls that the decision taken December 11th, 2008, regarding in particular the sharing of time for the witness Davor Marijan, was made after the expert report was examined and that the Chamber considered that one hour and thirty minutes was a sufficient time span as for the cross-examination on the part of the Petkovic Defence. Therefore, granting an hour and thirty minutes instead of thirty minutes, which had been granted to the Petkovic Defence, if the Chamber were to apply strictly paragraph 15 of the decision taken April 24th, 2008, the Chamber has been flexible in the overall granting of time for cross-examination on the part of the Petkovic Defence and has taken account of the particular characteristics of this report vis-à-vis the Petkovic Defence. In addition, the Chamber notes that the Petkovic Defence will, if need be, be able to contest the contents of the expert report, in particular when they present their case, by calling their own witnesses or, as the contested decision indicates, by calling this witness as a witness for its own case. Therefore, the Chamber does not see that there be any circumstances in the January 12th decision, 2009, which would compromise in any way the fairness and the speediness of the trial or its result; and therefore that this could enable the procedure to progress in keeping with Article 73(B) of the Rules and Regulations. Well, it was a very long text, indeed, but I had to read it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to thank you for your decision and for your dealing with all of our requests for additional time, which we have been repeatedly making. We would just like to state that none of the counsels [as interpreted] for Mr. Petkovic will talk about the Department of Defence. This is not our Defence strategy. We will not be addressing the same issues that will be addressed by this witness. Thank you once again for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I would like, at the very beginning, to see whether we have a correct translation of a very significant definition of the HVO that was provided by the witness. I'm talking about the term "blocking defence," as it was translated on page 31. It was translated as "blocking defence," so that was the term that was used in interpretation. My colleague suggested that a much more appropriate term for what the witness referred to, and it was also referred to in some other cases, is "final defence" or "critical defence."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So I would kindly ask the witness, if necessary, to explain one more time what this term in B/C/S "odsudna odbrana" actually means so that we can get a proper translation of the term.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am obliged, before I answer to this, to finalise my previous answer. When I spoke about the plan, I did see, for one of the HVO units towards the end of 1992, something that could be described as a defence plan. This had to do with the territory of Central Bosnia. And, similarly, in April or May 1993, also in Central Bosnia, I saw plans that were particularly defensive, and this also goes along with this term of "critical" or "decisive defence." I can confirm that I did see some notes, so only notes without elaboration, from the end of 1992, which according to my estimate were drafted in Tomislavgrad, and they referred to something that was a very broad plan of the defence of Kupres, which the HVO lost to the Serbs. So this is an addition to what I was saying. These are the only examples that I can confirm that I did see. So, indeed, even if you are -- if you are liberating a territory, you obviously will attack, but I never saw any elaboration of these notes. I apologise, but I felt obliged to mention this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, in order to have a precise interpretation, could you please tell us what the term used by you in your language, "odsudna odbrana," what does it mean, according to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This term is a military term which is used when you want to say that whoever is defending himself is now in a very unfavorable position, so possibly I might explain this by saying this is the defence on a single line. So you are literally on a cliff, and you are defending yourself facing a ravine. So I hope this was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be enough for the moment. I would just like to intervene with the transcript. Page 38, where we are using the term in B/C/S, this is with a B, "odsudna odbrana," rather than with the P as it stands right now.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is the final defence, actually, at the very last line. Though HVO actually never had two lines. It only had one, which says something about the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As regards the questions posed to you by Their Honours and what you were saying regarding the doctrine just before the break, there was a line of questions regarding Article 29(1), item 2. We were talking about the first part from item 2, which says: "... adopts the employment plan." You explained to the Chamber that according to you, HVO dealt with this decisive or final defence. Is this something that could be, according to you, related to a lack of doctrine, so can we make a correlation between this decisive or final defence and the lack of doctrine? I do not want to lead you in your answer any further, but if you are faced with such a final, decisive defence, do you actually have any time to develop a doctrine or do you have to do something more urgent?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I concluded here, and I believe I explained it in some other works of mine, that the basic characteristics of the HVO was the defence. It was a defence organisation, and this is truly its fundamental characteristic. So when you are defending yourself, there is an advantage to this. Defence is considered to be a stronger method of fighting, so it's easier, in other words, to defend oneself than to attack. This is partially true, but if you are only defending yourself and this defence is not elaborated thoroughly, then sometimes it can happen that whoever is attacking you will have full initiative. They will be able to choose time and place of the attacks, and this is exactly what happened to the HVO. And because of this unclear engagement or the impossibility to engage, you can find yourself in a position in which all of a sudden you will come to realise that you are actually faced with this final defence or critical defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, due to a range of questions that were raised, and the way in which you qualified the HVO, I would kindly ask you now to address a topic which I actually planned to address later on, and this is: In which way were these two decrees adopted? Could you please take a look at this binder X. So these are documents P289 - this is the Decree on the Armed Forces, adopted on July 3rd, 1992 - and in the same binder, document P00588, and this is the Decree on the Armed Forces adopted in October 1992. You are very familiar with these two decrees. Could you please explain to the Chamber what is the difference between these two decrees? We can see that they are different in volume, but actually these amendments were adopted relatively soon after the adoption of the original decree.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, as can be confirmed in Article 63, is based on the general National Defence of Yugoslavia Act of 1983 and the Act on Military Service from 1985. These acts, as you can see here, were amended on several occasions, but at this moment this is not too relevant. One thing that can be said about this decree from July 1992 is that it simply took over some of the provisions from the General People's Defence Act but not from the Act on Military Service. The second decree, however, took over also the provisions from the second-mentioned act, and this is why there is a difference also in approximately 110 additional articles. Why was this done in this way, I can't really tell you. There is also a rather strange formulation here, which could lead us to conclude that the acts are not being suspended by the adoption of these decrees, but only those parts which are contrary to the provisions of these decrees. In the largest part, the decree actually takes over all the articles, so the second decree takes over all the articles from the previous decree, but there are also some significant amendments of several articles, and they have to do with the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, so would we be correct to conclude that this second Decree on the Armed Forces, the document P00588, is actually a compilation of the Act on General People's Defence and the Act on Military Service that were effective prior to the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, we can say that because this decree took over a great deal of provisions from the previous two pieces of legislation. Obviously, it did not take over the provisions regarding the ideology of communist Yugoslavia and also certain responsibilities and obligations of certain executive bodies have been changed and accorded to the organisational structure of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you've seen these two decrees adopted by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You are familiar with the previous regulations. So do you believe that the Decree on the Armed Forces from October of 1992 is a satisfactory amalgamation of these two previous legislative acts?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: In my view, it is not. In my view, it would have been better to have two different decrees, one on the armed forces or defence, because the defence deals with a wider scope of issues. So I might say that in the HVO and in other armies, and in other societies and states created after the breakup of Yugoslavia, there was an attempt to remove themselves, as far as possible, from the ideology of the previous state, but these attempts were not all that successful. So HVO wanted to remove itself from the doctrine of the former Yugoslavia. This concept of general people's defence and social self-protection - this was its official title - this was actually a doctrine of armed people, and HVO declaretorily [as interpreted] tried to remove themselves from that, but this decree shows that they actually didn't do that, because you still have the so-called civilian defence, which was also one of the elements of the defence, you also have the -- you also have monitoring and alerting systems, so many elements, and the very title of the decree does not correspond to the content of the decree itself. This is why I believe that it would have been better, and certainly it would have been more precise, if they had two decrees instead of one. Why they opted for dissolution, I can only speculate, and there is no point in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, can you make a comparison? You mentioned these two decrees from the previous period that were actually merged into one, and they regulated the relations in the JNA. Can you explain to the Chamber or make a comparison between the JNA and the HVO? And in terms of that comparison, where would the position of the HVO be? Let me mention that this was dealt with by Mr. Pringle, too, and I would ask you for -- to provide arguments for your statements.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, whoever tries to make such a comparison and says that he or she did compare the HVO to the JNA either doesn't understand what they're talking about or they are not being honest about it because these two organisations are not comparable. Let me try to explain. First, I noticed here, in some expert opinions made for this Tribunal, that mostly, when talking about the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia, the term "JNA" is used. The JNA was not the military force of ex-Yugoslavia. The military force of ex-Yugoslavia were the armed forces of the SFRJ. They consisted of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. All these components were at an equal level. Let me mention that this was the only such example in the world. In all other cases, one component was dominant, either the territorial one, which was a rare example, or the operational component, which was much more frequent. But we can't go too deeply into the history of Yugoslavia, because that is not our subject matter here. Let me try to explain where it is possible to position the HVO in this system of armed forces, and I believe it can be positioned in that way. The JNA was a federal army. It has -- it had its peacetime personnel, that is, professionals, although they were never called that. They were officers, non-commissioned officers, and civilians serving the armed forces. And in terms of numbers, the farthest -- the stronger part of peacetime personnel were conscripts serving in the JNA. From 1985 or 1986 on, these conscripts were trained to become citizens able to engage in warfare in the case of a sudden aggression. And the wartime personnel of the JNA amounted to about a million, which is very strong, which is a very large number. So there was the JNA in its peacetime strength, as the first echelon, and the second echelon was -- were the reserve forces of the JNA. The Territorial Defence was organised by federal units, the republics. There was six republics and two provinces, and each had their own Territorial Defence. And what I'm about to say is really a literal quote. The Territorial Defence is the widest form of the mobilisation of the people and the population for combat. The difference between the JNA and the Territorial Defence was that the Territorial Defence was an exclusively wartime component. In peacetime, it had a very small number of officers, mostly in the municipalities. Every municipality of the former Yugoslavia had its own Territorial Defence staff that comprised three to five persons. Only in wartime would that structure grow. I know the example of Croatia, and there we're talking about the mobilisation of close to half a million people, apart from the Yugoslav People's Army. The Territorial Defence had its manoeuvre structure and its spatial structure. The manoeuvre structure of the Territorial Defence consisted of brigades, and the spatial structure consisted of the staffs in the municipalities, and different smaller units were linked to them or connected with them. The difference between the manoeuvre component and the spatial component was the following: The manoeuvre structure could be used outside the territory of the municipality from which the personnel were drafted, and even they could be used outside the territory of their republic, their federal unit, but the spatial structure would remain in their area. They are bound to its territory, and that's why they're called "spatial." If I were to rank them by value and under the criteria of equipment, armaments, et cetera, the armed forces of the SFRJ could be divided into four echelons: The first is the peacetime army; secondly, the reserve forces of the JNA; thirdly, the manoeuvre structure of the Territorial Defence; and, fourthly, the spatial structure of the Territorial Defence. So we can say that the spatial structure of the Territorial Defence is the only part of the armed forces that can be linked to the HVO, in terms of looking for its origin, how it came about. So this is the only thing that can be compared, actually. Let me mention the characteristics of the spatial structure. The strong influence of local political and party structures because all appointments of officials, the equipment of those forces were duties of those municipalities, were within the remit of the municipalities. And the third characteristic is the defence nature of those forces, defensive nature. As we progress, I believe that we will find corroboration for these statements of mine in my opinion, unless you want me to do some now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of what you've just said, I'd like to ask you a very specific question, and you can possibly answer. Let's take a theoretical case. A 22-year-old person who's a Muslim and lives in Mostar. He knows he's in a country called the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He knows that this Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has an army, BiH. He knows that there is the Territorial Defence and so on. He also knows that there is a decree adopted by HVO which is likely -- which would make him enlist as an HVO soldier. So this young 22-year-old Muslim boy, what is he to do? Join his country's army? Join the HVO? How can he solve the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do allow me to answer your question, taking the example of Livno, which has been mentioned already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take Livno.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. As regards the Livno Muslims, I was a member of one of the stronger HVO brigades, in terms of personnel strength. Until July 1993, I believe it had six battalions. An entire battalion was made up of Muslim soldiers, and there were Muslim soldiers the other battalions also, but in those other battalions they were a minority. A 22-year-old Muslim man had the opportunity to choose. He would have had three options: One, to join the Muslim Battalion of the Livno Brigade, which also had insignia of the BiH Army, apart from the HVO insignia; option 2 would be to join another battalion with a Croatian majority; and there was also the option for him to leave the municipality and join a pure unit, if I may call it that, of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just said something that I am hearing for the first time, and therefore it's of particular interest to me. The brigade had six battalions, and therefore there was a battalion composed totally of Muslims, and you added a small detail which I've never heard thus far. You said that in that battalion, aside from the HVO insignia, they also had the insignia of the BiH on their clothing. Is that the case, and how long did that continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It really was that way, Your Honour. I know not because I was in the sector of that battalion, but for the simple reason that in my free time I would meet some individuals of that battalion in town, people who had been at school with me, and they did wear those insignia. I cannot say that this was the case in other parts of Herceg-Bosna. The mayor of Livno was a very tolerant man, and he certainly wouldn't have insisted that the army, upon which he exerted a great influence, remove these insignia. I will immediately add when I observed that. Since September 1992, up until mid-July 1993, I was not at Livno. Whether in the meantime they had removed these insignia, I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Since these were your school-mates, you said you knew some of them, I imagine you had the opportunity to talk with them, what was their state of mind, given that there was the Croatian Community that existed, the HVO, the army of the HVO, and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was there sort of a schizophrenic atmosphere, they didn't really know where they were at, or did they have the impression that the HVO was a component of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it really wasn't a problem for them? In particular, what was their state of mind when they knew that between the HVO and the BiH, there were confrontations perhaps elsewhere, perhaps not in Livno, but perhaps elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wouldn't be telling the truth if I were to say that we discussed these issues. We were young boys at the time, and we mostly met in cafes and watched girls. That was our upper-most interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can understand that, indeed, that you be interested in girls. Everyone understands that, but yet there was a political situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speak about 1992, and in that year I did not have the impression that people of my generation, at least, were bothered by that. They still had much influence in business and in the authorities, and nobody can say that they were really discriminated against, et cetera. But later on, of course, the confrontations that happened in other municipalities in 1993, which I know from stories that I heard later - I wasn't there, down there at the time - that all that had an impact, that there was dissatisfaction, and that there was -- that there were divisions. I can mention a naive relative of mine, as an example, who was a company commander in Livno. And roughly about the time of when the clashes between the HVO and the BiH army began, went to Bugojno, which is a good 100 kilometres away, and he was taken prisoner at the check-point, of course. Later on, he was released and didn't have any problems because he had his notebook on him with a list of his soldiers, and some of them were Muslims. I know that he told me later that he didn't have problems on account of that.
