So this goes to show that there was a strong local focus in all the communities that people didn't really care what was going on in, I don't know, three municipalities away or so. But, of course, in July 1993 the Muslims in the HVO were disarmed, that's a fact, for preventative reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to return to some issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If we could finish the topic that we were talking about. You were making a comparison between the HVO and the JNA and you said that the HVO had a spatial structure and that they were a defensive army. Would you please explain to the Chamber whether the HVO had professional forces and how they fit into this picture you are painting?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The HVO did have professionals in its ranks. There was a regiment and a number of battalions and companies. I was in a brigade that was a successor of a professional regiment. I know that their nominal strength were 2.860 men, but I know that they never had over 460 infantry. Sorry, I said "400 infantry," 400 infantry. In all, the HVO had about a thousand or 1100 professional soldiers to counter that. That's a category that did not exist in the former system, and they were meant to be a manoeuvre forces, but with a thousand or 1100 men. Well, it is clear from the number that they weren't much of a manoeuvre force, and they were not all in the same territory. Another characteristic of theirs was that they were infantry units with light weapons. Up until the summer of 1993, at least, the regiment that I mentioned got its first 120-millimetre mortar. That was the heaviest armament that they had. So for a year, they fought with weapons the calibre of which did not exceed 60 millimetres, and that's the calibre of a small mortar. The reserve brigades had greater fire-power, and they made up the majority of the forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to indicate the fact that since time is of the essence, I would like to ask the Registrar whether we can continue without a break until 17 minutes after 6.00, and then we will have a break. So we can continue until 17 minutes past 6.00 without taking a second break, and that will enable us to gain 20 minutes in our time. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me now return to some issues that are important and follow from the questions of Judge Antonetti about the young man in Livno. You said that in July, the Bosniaks, for preventive reasons, were disarmed in the HVO. This is something we didn't deal with in this expert opinion, but let me ask you to be more precise about that. How do you know about it, what did you know about it, what documentation did you see, but briefly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the history of the HVO as a military component, there is a watershed, if I may call it that, after which nothing was ever the same again on that day, the 30th of June, 1993. On that day, a significant part of the Muslims of the 2nd Brigade of the HVO in Mostar betrayed their comrades and crossed the line to join the BiH Army, a consequence of which was the fall of the barracks, apart from any other problems, and that was a warning to everybody else. And there was a risk, the risk of keeping Muslims in HVO units was too great from that moment on; and the HVO, which until then had been the military formation with the greatest share of members of other ethnicities, was to enter into an almost mono-ethnic formation, apart from the Orasje district, but the Orasje district is not relevant here, I believe. But in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslims were being disarmed from that day on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Briefly, do you have knowledge, based on the documents you saw, that the ethnic Croats participated in HVO units in territories controlled by the BiH Army, and together with them fought the Serbian Army? Do you have such knowledge? We -- and if you know about such territories, please mention them.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Units of the HVO and territories where Muslims were dominant, well, there were HVO units in Sarajevo, first and foremost, Sarajevo and then Tuzla. There were brigade-level units there, and they continued to function as HVO for a while after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, thank you. In connection with this, and we'll get there yet, until the 30th of June, 1993, did you see any documents about the number of Muslims in HVO units? I mean the numbers for the period until the 30th of June, 1993. We will show a document later. As a historian who had the chance to compare information about persons belonging to other ethnicities and other armies, such as the Serbian Army or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you say what the share of Muslims was in HVO units until June the 30th, 1993? I am specifically referring to Herzegovina now.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I think that in my report, you can find a document of that kind. It dates from the beginning of June 1993, and it depicts the share of Muslims in the HVO. I believe it was over 16 percent. Out of that number, most of them were in the Operative Zone Eastern Herzegovina, that is, the valley of the Neretva River, Livno, to a lesser extent in Central Bosnia, and there were many in Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll look at that document later, going through your report, as well as many other documents, but I want this to be clear on the record. You personally saw these people, these Muslim friends of yours, who wore on their sleeves at the same time the coat of arms of the Republic of Croatia [as interpreted] and the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes. I have -- I have one of those patches in my collection, half HVO, half ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Those were local Muslims who joined the defence effort?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, mainly from Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And who were they fighting, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me there must be a mistake on line 6. Did you say the patches of the HVO and not the Republic of Croatia? Otherwise, we would have the impression that we're talking about soldiers of the Republic of Croatia who were on site. Line 6, page 52, must be "the coat of arms of the HVO and the BiH," it seems to me. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, correct, that's exactly what I asked, coat of arms of the HVO and coat of arms of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said, Witness, something which is very important to us here. You made a connection, when you were talking about spatial structures between them and a certain municipality. You linked them to a strong political and party influence on the local level, and you said that the mayor of Livno was a fair-minded man, a decent man who would have never had a problem with anyone wearing that kind of insignia. Now, a follow-up question would be about the influence of municipalities on the armed forces and on the HVO, because you talk about that in your report in several places, and I believe it's very important to explain here the influence of municipalities. Could you give us more detail?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, after several stages of the founding and establishment of the HVO, there existed municipal staffs of the HVO which were renamed from TO municipal staffs. At the beginning, they were headed by people appointed by municipalities, and thus it happened that several months later, when the system was already gaining a definite shape, some structures were already in existence that were greatly under the influence of municipalities and they were funded by municipalities. We could see that the kind of thinking, the kind of perception that the HVO as a municipal force, answerable to the municipalities, but in my opinion the real strength, the real power of the municipalities, was that heads of municipalities were presidents of local communities, so there were at the same time chiefs on the HVO level, and they were represented on the legislative level. I think that is a bizarre solution, and I've never seen anything like that anywhere else, but that's how it was. Therein lies the key to the great power of municipalities over the HVO, and that also explains great resistance to decentralisation -- to centralisation. And writing this report, I came to the conclusion that Herceg-Bosna would be best defined as a union of loosely-connected municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, what you've just said is important. It's not the first time that this topic has been discussed, and I'd like to profit from the fact that you were here, because you were present in Livno and also because you know a number of people. In your opinion, the local individuals, these VIPs who composed the Presidency, compared to Mr. Boban, because of the number of these individuals in Livno, in Mostar and elsewhere because they were so numerous, did they have an influence on Boban to the extent that Boban simply executed orders or decisions made by these local leaders, or, on the basis of the military documents that you have had the opportunity to examine, was Boban the man executing orders, and the local leaders were in the background so to speak? What is your impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the intensity and the frequency of meetings between Boban, as president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and presidents of municipalities gives us a clear answer to this question. As far as I know, in 1992 the Presidency convened for the last time on the 17th October 1992, and I remember that date because that's the date when the amendment to this Decree on the Armed Forces was passed, and I cannot remember seeing that the Presidency met again before the end of April 1993. It is my impression that everybody was happy in their own backyard, and I cannot guarantee, of course, that Boban tried to convene sessions and they resisted - I haven't seen it on paper - but the rarity of their meetings at that time leads me to conclude that the policy being followed was, Don't rock the boat and everyone stick to your own municipality. I know it's very difficult to define how much influence Boban really wielded, because I have seen very few documents of that nature, very few documents that could enlighten us in that way. I heard things from people who knew him, but in my profession that is called hearsay, and you must always allow the possibility that people have their own ulterior motives for saying whatever they're saying. But I don't think any of them held Mr. Boban in very high esteem. Some people even told me that apart from his own municipality, he wasn't interested in much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, I asked you, and I'd like you to come back to the gist of my question, about the influence of municipalities on the HVO military structure. You said that the Community of Herceg-Bosna was a union of loosely-connected states, and if I can paraphrase, each municipality was a state within a state, and you told us that municipalities were territorially defined. But tell us now about 1992 and 1993. What was the attitude of those local chiefs and officials towards the HVO and towards the financing of the HVO at this central level? And we'll turn later to some other details.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The influence of municipalities, from the outbreak of the conflict with Serbs and the conflagration of the war in April 1992 until the founding of local bodies, municipalities had already gained a considerable power over defence structures, but it was an inherited power. It was nothing new, this influence they had over local structure. They had money, and they were the main sources of funding for these forces. And that turned out to be a problem later because members of the HVO were not all equally paid, for the simple reason that some municipalities were richer than others. And as new appointments proceeded, it became more and more difficult to follow a definite staffing policy because that led to a conflict with municipalities, and municipalities were not subordinate to the HVO. Therefore, it was a conflict with the leader of the municipality, who was also a member of the Presidency of the HZ-HB. In the summer and autumn of 1992, local staffs were, for the most part, renamed into brigades. In the system which gave me my military education and training, a brigade is considered to be a composite unit that is not linked to a specific territory. However, from later developments, you see that there was a huge resistance to the idea that HVO units should go outside their territory. They simply didn't want to, and it was only with enormous efforts from the Main Staff that certain units started moving in the autumn 1993 and the winter of 1993-1994. That is another proof of their essentially defensive nature. You can call it what you want. You can call a car a Mercedes, but if it's not a Mercedes, it will not perform like one. And you could say the same about the units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marijan. These issues you're talking about, the influence of local authorities, did you notice that this caused problems with mobilisation and other ways of catering to the HVO and supplying it, depending on the municipality in question, its wealth, but also on the leader of the municipality, who may have had a different concept of defending his area?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I have seen a large number of documents from which you can see that municipalities were striving for the greatest possible independence. At one session of the HVO on the 14th October 1992, the president of the HVO, the head of the HVO, said that municipalities were acting like states, and at a later session in 1993, it was said that little had changed; the municipalities had to contribute from their budget to the Defence Department. But I have never seen any document about this. In the Municipality of Livno, maybe it had nothing to contribute. I know that on the example of Livno, the brigade was paid until the end of 1992 from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, 1993. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So to reiterate, you know that the brigade in Livno, until the end of 1993, was paid by the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Perhaps it's better to say until the autumn of 1993 because I'm not sure if it's October or November.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's not split hairs. It's partly autumn, partly winter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a question which is in line with what has just been asked. You remained in those units. You know that there was the so-called Croatian Community. Then there was the Republic of Herceg-Bosna; right? When that transition took place, and when the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was founded, in -- what happened in the minds of the soldiers? What did they think, "We are a republic as we were under the former Yugoslavia," that is, the state was Yugoslavia, and there was the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia, so it didn't change much at the end of the day, or the foot soldier or the officer or yourselves had the feeling that something new was created -- was established which eventually would become a state? How did you experience this transition? And you were on the spot, of course, but you're also an expert and you managed to review documents, and perhaps there are documents which may help you answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have to go back a little. In fact, we have to go back all of 20 years. Over that time, I was in the Students Platoon of the Livno Brigade, and it was a peculiar unit. It just crossed my mind, I was commander of that platoon in the independent sector held by a company, and it was a residual platoon of the HOS that had stripped itself of its insignia, and there was even a platoon of waiters and a platoon of students; a rather mixed company, you would say. And you have to believe me when I say that I really don't remember either my own reaction or any of my colleagues' to the announcement that Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent republic. We in Herzegovina never discussed it. What bothered me a little, perhaps, is something that in 1992 and 1993 never happened, was that somebody would come to us soldiers and explain something, so the members of this Students Platoon of the Livno Brigade were totally uninformed about this political decision and its political goal. From what I know from the documents, I would say that Herceg-Bosna and its armed forces lived from day to day, and that's something that bothered the Muslims more than others. But in the circle of my acquaintance, and I must say I'm not sure that circle is representative, in the circle of my acquaintances I said the indifference to this was complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to take you back to your expert report and your findings. We left off at something very important, the material replenishment of the HVO. Could you tell us very briefly about the tasks of the HVO, and we can talk about the Decree on the Armed Forces up to Article 50, because the provisions on readiness are very similar, and about the second decree as well. What were the main tasks?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I commented on the tasks of the HVO in Chapter 4 based on these decrees. Its task was to implement the defence policy and to conduct preparations for the defence of Herceg-Bosna. So there was a plan of defence of Herceg-Bosna. And let me emphasise it's not a war plan, because the plan of defence encompasses the whole society, determining measures for improving defence, identifying sources of finance, et cetera. I won't read on. You can see it in the report. And, of course, one of its fundamental obligations was to provide material supplies to armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: According to both Decrees on Armed Forces, let us take the one on the 3rd of July, what were the tasks of defence -- of the Defence Department, rather, under this decree?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The Defence Department -- excuse me. Do you mean only the stipulations?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's paragraph 5 in your report. I mean only the provisions of the Decree on the Armed Forces. We'll get to Article 10 when it becomes necessary.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The Defence Department of the HZ-HB was an organ dealing with administrative and professional tasks within the sphere of defence and security. That's its official definition.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When do we find the first reference to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: In May 1992, in the statutory decision on the provisional structure of the executive power in the HZ-HB, and it was amended on the 3rd of July 1992. Later, when I speak about this statutory decision, I also mention the amended decision specifically with a view to the Defence Department because it was only established right then on the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Speaking of provisions to the armed forces, what is the principal task of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The principal responsibility of the Defence Department was providing material and supplies to the armed forces; that is, weapons, equipment, and other military materiel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what was its secondary responsibility, and together with whom?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: "Secondary" is a good word. It performed it together with other defence bodies, because this was wartime, after all. And in view of the extent of the purview, other bodies had other responsibilities; providing food, medical responsibilities, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Which article is that? I'm talking about paragraph 6 of your report, which article governs these responsibilities of the Defence Department providing combat and other equipment in cooperation with other bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: It's Article 41.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. That suffices for now. I would like now to move on. We've dealt with the influence of municipalities, and now you can concentrate on the second part of your report, which is called -- entitled "Defence Department." Could you explain to the Judges when the Defence Department was created, what preceded it, and why it was set up?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The Department of Defence was established to carry out administrative and professional tasks from the domain of defence and security. It was established on the 3rd of July, 1992, and started functioning then. So it was established when there were some structures of the HVO. The necessity for it had been known for quite a time. I have mentioned the statutory decision dated May the 15th, but from that decision until the creation of the defence, two months had to elapse. The best example of why it was necessary to the HVO can be seen in a document which is a letter dated 28th of June, 1992, where many tasks are listed that should be carried out by the Department of Defence, so as to unburden the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We will have to reduce the number of documents I want to show you, because we are making very slow progress. Let me just ask you whether you are referring to document P279 in binder 1, and you said that it was on the 20th of June, but the document reads the 26th of June. Is this the document you have mentioned a short while ago, so binder 1, the following document, this should be it? I can tell from here.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document. It's -- it is a good depiction of the situation and about the municipalities. This shows also to what extent the HVO is a defence force. Even in the case of luck at the front-line, they do not continue to advance, which is, militarily speaking, almost suicide if you fail to build upon your successes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We did note here the Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The last two paragraphs on page 1 in the Croatia text; right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How does it begin?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: After the shock that the enemy had to bear, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Marijan, in your report you deal with issues that Judge Prandler has mentioned, and these are contained in Article 10 of the decree, so let us show what the tasks of the Presidency of the HZ-HB were in defence matters and what were the tasks of the HVO to the HZ-HB. What does Article 10 say, and is it identical, when we speak about the versions from July and October 1992 respectively?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Article 10 makes a list of 24 duties of the Department of Defence, and the decree of the 3rd of July mentions 25, but only because item 6 is actually omitted. So this was corrected subsequently. I believe that the list is completely identical, but let me add that the duties of the Department of Defence cannot be understood if Article 10 is viewed in isolation without connection to Article 11, because only that latter article makes it clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, let us make an analysis. I hope that we will be able to do so in the remaining 20 minutes. Let us see what the duties of the Department of Defence were and whether the Department of Defence, according to the documents that you saw, did anything to implement them, and how would you characterize these duties the way they are listed here, and what they mean, in rough terms? Let us start with -- let me remind you we're looking at document P00588, so it is in binder X. So the document is P00588. We're looking at Article 10, because here the numbering is correct. Please put it in front of you so you don't have to turn around and you don't have to turn away from the microphone. Tell me, please, what you mean by task number 1: "Monitoring and coordinating activities aimed at achieving the agreed policy of the defence system and presenting measures aimed at gaining necessary momentum for the development and eventual realisation within the HZ-HB." I will always ask you to say if this was indeed done by the Department of Defence and whether that is really a task that the Department of Defence should realise.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and I believe I saw some documents about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us continue with item 2: "Assessing possible wartime and other dangers."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This item, when it comes to other dangers, the assessment of other dangers, is certainly within the remit of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us continue with 3: "Making plans on the use of armed forces."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: That is not a task of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you -- can you elaborate?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Can I continue, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It seems that my question coincides with what Judge Prandler wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't know what Judge Prandler -- whether he wanted to say something. I am Judge Trechsel, for your information, if you were referring to me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: My mistake. Apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. It was an interpreter's involuntary practical joke. I'm sorry. I think I also want to hear more about this, and you seem to go into that direction, and you have priority of course, Ms. Nozica. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's exactly what I wanted to say. I suppose that my additional question was in line with the question you wanted to ask. I'm rather sure I did not mention any names.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So when we speak about assessments, we were discussing item 3: "Making plans on the use of armed forces." You said that this was not the task of the Department of Defence, and I asked you to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I think that what I have just said is best explained by explaining Articles 10 and 11. Otherwise, confusion may arise, and we don't want that. Article 10, that provides for the rights and duties of the Department of Defence, can only be interpreted correctly if we know the content of Article 11. Paragraph 2 in Article 10, which says that the Defence Department performs these tasks, in Article 11 we can see that for the carrying out of these tasks, the Main Staff is being established. Only then can we proceed to these 24 tasks, because they -- they fall either under the Main Staff or under the Commander-in-Chief, but not under the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you said the following: In order to determine precisely what the tasks of the Department of Defence or other bodies were, that the Department of Defence carries out staff and other technical work --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would kindly ask the Defence counsel to read less fast, if she has to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may finish. I am reading and speaking as slowly that I believe I'll go on for -- I'll go on all week, so I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So we have to see this in connection with Article 11, which says that for the carrying out of the tasks set out in Article 10, paragraph 2, that the Main Staff is established; is that so, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I hate to [indiscernible] good at the computers. I would like to read what our expert, Mr. Marijan, has said, and then I will lose that if you continue. So let me then -- let me then point out the following: Mr. Marijan said that paragraph 2 in Article 10, which says that the Defence Department performs these tasks, in Article 11 we can see that for the carrying out of these tasks, the Main Staff is being established: "Only then can we proceed to these 24 tasks, because they -- they fall either the under the Main Staff or under the Commander-in-Chief, but not under the Department of Defence." End of the quotation. Frankly, I do not understand this. Then how come Article 10 says in the preamble that the Defence Department shall engage in activities pertaining to, and then we will have the 25 tasks? And that is true that afterwards Article 11 specifies and points out that, and I quote: "In order to perform the tasks stipulated in paragraph 2, Article 10 of this decree ..." And let me then again emphasise the tasks stipulated in paragraph 2, Article 10 of this decree, that is, the department, the Main Staff shall be established within the Defence Department, that is true, but again I say that in my view all these articles should be read and understood -- I mean, Articles 10, 11 and 29, whatever that was, 29, they should be read and understood and interpreted as a common basis about the defence forces and about the tasks of the defence. I stand to be corrected, if you so wish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you said, Your Honour, is correct. These three articles are deeply interconnected, and Article 11 cannot be understood properly without Article 29. Article 10 lists a number of duties, and let me correct myself. These are, first and foremost, duties of the supreme commander. There are ten of them, and they are all -- almost all are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you have now said something completely different from what Judge Prandler wanted to say, so let me state the following: Judge Prandler said that there was Article 10, there is Article 29, there is Article 9, that stipulates which bodies have to do, and he said we have to do that separately.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I apologise. I had the impression --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment. So Judge Prandler wants to say, if I understood him correctly, and I assume I did, that Article 10 makes a list of the duties of the Department of Defence in 24 items. Mr. Marijan, I'm not going to ask you questions about the interpretation of law. We know that legal provisions can only be interpreted by the Chamber. But I'll ask you, item by item, whether you observed that the Department of Defence actually did that or why you did -- why you think that this is -- should not be part of the duties of the Department of Defence. And whenever you think that a task was delegated or attributed to some other body and some other provision, please say so. So there is the drafting of plans and the employment of the armed forces. Is that a task of the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Whose task is that, do you think?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: That is a task of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, sir, this question of the Chief of Staff, which is an important issue in terms of the chain of command, we see, under Article 10, the Department of Defence is responsible for 24 tasks, but then Article 11 states that the Chief of Staff is created within the Department of Defence or inside the Department of Defence. Therefore, this Chief of Staff, under Article 10 and Article 11, comes under the responsibility of the head of the Department of Defence, and this Chief of Staff, the structure of which has been defined by the Commander-in-Chief, Mr. Boban, is going to appoint the general who will be the head of the Chief of Staff, but that applies during times of peace. But in times of war, it would seem that there is a different structure, which is the War Cabinet. Since we are talking here about the chain of responsibility, we have to be certain that everyone understands this, that all of the Judges understand this because if we were to make a mistake, that would have consequences. According to what you have studied, was this Chief of Staff integrated into the Department of Defence? And if that was the case, if it's integrated, then the chief -- the head of the Chief of Staff is subordinated to the head of the Department of Defence, in other words, the minister of defence? This is the question I put to you. I don't have the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the General Staff or Main Staff of the HVO is a part of the Department of Defence, but its a part of the Department of Defence that has dual remit. I explained that in my report. It is subordinate to the supreme commander for some issues, and the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, could the witness be asked to repeat this part of his answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The interpreter is asking you to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the HVO is part of the Defence Department, which we can see from the decree, and it was headed by the chief of the Main Staff, who was responsible for administrative and professional affairs, but he was answerable to the president of the HZ-HB. So the Main Staff had a special position in the area of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just say that once again we have an incomplete interpretation. The witness said that the chief of the Main Staff was answerable to the head of the Defence Department inasmuch as technical and professional affairs were concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, sir, this is an important matter. Everyone realises that this is an important question. We cannot continue at this hour of the day, for reasons of our schedule. We will all have the entire night to rethink this matter, and Madam Nozica, tomorrow at 9.00, will be able to continue asking questions on this very issue. Mr. Witness, sir, you have taken the solemn oath, and therefore you must have no contact with the Defence or with anyone. The only thing you can do is to inform your wife that everything is going well; nothing more. I am giving you these instructions to avoid any potential problem. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. We will be meeting in the morning, and we will most likely continue with these very matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I really have to say this for the transcript. If I were allowed to go at least through these principal founding documents, and I believe I will be able to do that within the first half hour tomorrow, then at least when we have gone through the founding documents and what was being done in the Defence Department, it will be much easier to ask questions, and we could go through the matter more swiftly, because you are now invoking documents that I have yet to show the witness. I will show them tomorrow, and then we can focus on issues that are the most important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine. We all agree on that. We shall have a 30-minute break at this point and resume in a different format that I informed you of. I won't say any more, because this is a public hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be followed by an Ex Parte Hearing. The hearing will reconvene on Tuesday, the 20th day of January, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.16 p.m.,
